q-114051:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{|\sqrt{5}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{5}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{5}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{5}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{|\sqrt{5}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{5}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{5}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\sqrt{5}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{5}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-114052:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|\sqrt{2}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{2}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{2}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{|\sqrt{2}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{2}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-19393:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5}{\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{16\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/16)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/16}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/4)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{4})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{4}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5}{\sqrt{16-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/4)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (4\,\text{d}u) \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =5\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =5\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2})-5\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

q-104536:
First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y+z=1 \\ 2x-2y-2z=2 \\ -2x+2y+4z=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =0|\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =0-(8-4)+(4-4) \\  & =-4+0 \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -4 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{-4}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x+y+z=2+1+0=3.$
